subject: mathematics
question_text: If A + B + C = π, show that sin(A/2) + sin(B/2) − sin(C/2) = −1 + 4 cos((π − A)/4) cos((π − B)/4) sin((π − C)/4).

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), book p.100, chapter 8 TRANSFORMATIONS, Long Answer question 3(iii). The book prints TRANSFORMATIONS as a separate un-numbered chapter-style banner immediately after chapter 8's VSAQ run and restarts its numbering at 1; we ship both under one unit, ordered by the syllabus, and never mirror the book's arrangement. The leading −1 on the right-hand side was checked separately and is correct as printed: it comes from sin(C/2) = cos((π−C)/2) = 1 − 2sin²((π−C)/4), whose −1 survives the factorisation. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+3+2+1+1 split rewards the two substantial transformations — the sum-to-product pairing and the use of the angle condition — over the set-up and the finish, and it is the same split and the same step ids already carried by the sibling cards of this family (sin2a_sum, cos2a_sum, sin_half_squares, cos_half_squares), deliberately: they are ONE method over different identities, so a student who learns the arc once can attempt any of them. IDENTITY CHECKED NUMERICALLY before and after writing, and every intermediate line of the derivation with it: at A = 50°, B = 60°, C = 70° both sides equal 0.3490418254, and the identity holds again at (40°, 75°, 65°) and (110°, 25°, 45°). Paper position: Maths-1A Section C carries the long answers at 8 marks each under the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27), any 2 of 3; the Transformations slot is always a question of this kind. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. The right-hand side is built from QUARTER angles, so the condition is not only stated but divided by 4 before it is used.
steps.memory_tip: Every argument on the right has a 4 under it, so divide the condition by 4: (A+B)/4 = (π−C)/4.
lines: A + B + C = π  ⇒  A + B = π − C

recall.must_convey: That the condition is divided by 4, giving (A+B)/4 = (π−C)/4, because the right-hand side is in quarter angles.
accept: divide the angle sum by four to get A plus B over four equals pi minus C over four
quarter the condition because the answer is in quarter angles
write the condition down and bring it to quarter angles
condition ni four tho divide chesi, A plus B by four equals pi minus C by four rasi
state the given condition in quarter angle form

steps.why: The condition can only be substituted into an expression of the same size, so it is brought down to quarter angles at the start.
common_mistakes: Halving the condition instead of quartering it.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. Pair the two PLUS terms; averaging two half angles is where the quarter angles appear. Then sin(C/2) is rewritten in the form that carries the −1 the answer begins with.
steps.memory_tip: Choose sin(C/2) = 1 − 2sin²((π−C)/4). The 1 in it becomes the −1 in the answer.
lines: [∵ sin p + sin q = 2 sin((p+q)/2) cos((p−q)/2)]

recall.must_convey: That sin(A/2) and sin(B/2) are paired with the sin C + sin D formula, and sin(C/2) is written as 1 − 2sin²((π−C)/4).
accept: pair the two plus terms with the sine sum formula, which gives quarter angles
apply sum to product on sin A over two and sin B over two
write sin C over two as one minus two sin squared pi minus C over four
modati rendu plus terms ni pair cheyyali, sin C by two ni one minus two sin square ga rasi
expand sin C over two so the one appears

steps.why: The answer begins with −1, and that −1 has to be produced. Writing sin(C/2) as 1 − 2sin²((π−C)/4) and subtracting it is where it comes from.
common_mistakes: Using cos 2θ = 2cos²θ − 1, which gives the wrong sign on the constant.
Applying the sine SUM formula to a pair where one term carries a minus sign.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. The quartered condition replaces (A+B)/4 by (π−C)/4, and the expansion of sin(C/2) is substituted; subtracting it leaves the −1 outside.
steps.memory_tip: Subtracting 1 − 2sin²((π−C)/4) gives −1 plus a positive square term. The −1 stays outside from here on.

recall.must_convey: That (A+B)/4 is replaced by (π−C)/4 and the expansion of sin(C/2) is subtracted, which puts the −1 outside.
accept: replace A plus B over four by pi minus C over four
subtract the expansion so minus one appears and the square term turns positive
substitute the condition and the expansion of sin C over two
A plus B by four ni pi minus C by four ga marchali, minus one bayata vasthundi
use the quartered condition to convert the first term

steps.why: The condition converts an expression in A and B into one in C, and the subtraction turns the 1 into the −1 the answer needs.
common_mistakes: Subtracting only the 1 and leaving the sign of 2sin²((π−C)/4) unchanged.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. The −1 is set aside, 2 sin((π−C)/4) comes out, and the sine inside the bracket is turned into a cosine so that both bracket terms are cosines.
steps.memory_tip: Inside the bracket, sin((π−C)/4) = cos((π+C)/4), and the condition rewrites that as cos((2π−A−B)/4).

recall.must_convey: That −1 is kept outside, 2 sin((π−C)/4) is taken out, and sin((π−C)/4) inside the bracket is rewritten as cos((2π−A−B)/4).
accept: keep the minus one outside and take two sin pi minus C over four common
rewrite the sine inside the bracket as a cosine using sine theta equals cos of pi by two minus theta
the bracket becomes cos A minus B over four plus cos two pi minus A minus B over four
minus one bayata unchi, two sin pi minus C by four common teeyyali
convert the sine so both bracket terms are cosines

steps.why: A formula only applies when both bracket terms are the same kind of function, and the bracket must be a SUM of cosines to give the product of cosines the answer needs.
common_mistakes: Writing sin θ = cos(π/2 + θ), which puts a minus sign in.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The cosine SUM formula turns the bracket into a product of two quarter-angle cosines. Half the sum gives (π−B)/4 and half the difference gives −(π−A)/4; cosine is an even function, so the minus sign disappears.
steps.memory_tip: Half the sum is (π−B)/4 and half the difference is −(π−A)/4. Cosine is even, so the minus sign drops.
lines: [∵ cos p + cos q = 2 cos((p+q)/2) cos((p−q)/2)]

recall.must_convey: That the cosine sum formula turns the bracket into 2 cos((π−A)/4) cos((π−B)/4), giving −1 + 4 cos((π−A)/4) cos((π−B)/4) sin((π−C)/4).
accept: apply the cosine sum formula to get two cos pi minus A over four times cos pi minus B over four
half the sum is pi minus B over four and half the difference is pi minus A over four
the bracket becomes a product of two quarter angle cosines and the minus one stays
cos sum formula tho two cos pi minus A by four cos pi minus B by four vasthundi
the final answer is minus one plus four cos pi minus A by four cos pi minus B by four sin pi minus C by four

steps.why: A sum of two cosines is a product of two cosines. Averaging (A−B)/4 with (2π−A−B)/4 gives (π−B)/4, and their half difference gives (π−A)/4 once the even property of cosine is used.
common_mistakes: Using the cosine difference formula, which would give sines.
Losing the leading −1 at the very end.
